SANDF horses

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
should horses be entrusted into the care of the SANDF?

Unique Selling Point:
In Aug 2018 the Nspca were horrified to discover that horses in the care of the SANDF at their equine base called SAASIC in Potchestroom army base were starving to death. Over 200 hundred horses had been purchased by the army for the new SAASIC unit - these horses were to be trained for border patrol. There is a long history with regard to horses in the SANDF, going back to their use in border patrol in the 1970's and 1980"s. The unit had been disbanded and the police took over the care of horses for their use. Then SAASIC was formed in 2014. Most of the horses that were bought were not tame. and the NSPCA offered help to the army. to help train the horses. This was turned down. They heard reports of the animals being mistreated and went to investigate. many of the horses were not being fed...and some were in such bad condition that 25 had to be put down immediately., Whilst the NCPCA were there they saw army riding horses in a cruel way, and they filmed this. 2 charges were laid for animal cruelty. They also got a court order preventing the riders from riding these horses. The NSPCA did a deal with the Army and took over the care of 76 horses which they re-homed. In a matter of months these untame horses became tame. A vet did an experiment on the horses back at the base. The vet showed different uniforms to the horses that had been abused..the only uniform that the horses reacted badly to was sandf uniforms. The SANDF insisted on keeping some horses at their base but against the advice of the NSPCA, the SANDF sent 60 to an army base called Rooiwal, better conditions. They were warned about this because of the high incidence of equine sickness in the area. The army insisted. 20 horses died with the year from equine sickness and many broke their legs because if then rough terrain. Its been a year since charges were laid but the progress of the investigation has been hampered by lack of SANDF o-operation. A commission of enquiry was held apparently by the army into the starving horses but the results of this enquiry were not released. There is a rumour that the SANDF paid top dollar for trained horses but instead they received untrained horses.,

Summary:
There is a natural narrative - and the overriding theme is the care and protection of animals whether they are in service or our pets. We expect the state to set an example. The SANDF's treatment of these horses is nothing short of a scandalous. Two charges against the SANDF speaks volumes.
Our story line should send shivers down the spine of our viewers and it is hoped that there will be such an outcry that radical attitude changes will result at the SANDF.

Further information:
We can have access to the duplicate police docket. Pictures of the herd. Pictures of the horses that were put down. Pics of the horses that were cruelly kicked by SANDF riders. Their logo - Kick The Meat Forward. Pics of dud horses that were acquired, like a one eyed horse. - videos of 67 horses being rounded up at the base, driven away and put into a lovely green field. Then taken to new owners. Video of an experiment by a vat to show how the horses were terrified by a SANDF uniform. Hopefully ten second video of the horses being kicked. Hopefully a horse that was out down last month by the vet in Rooiwal.

Press Release:


The SANDF’s Horses
Starving, infected with various diseases and some eating their own faeces, over 25 horses have had to be put down after being in the care of the South African Army Special Infantry Capability Unit at the SANDF’s Potchefstroom base last year. A further 22 horses rescued from the base had to be euthanised as they were in such poor condition. Carte Blanche investigates why 11 of the 60 horses which the SANDF transferred to another army base in Pretoria have died and we visit some of the surviving horses that have been re-homed, while the NSPCA laid cruelty charges in terms of the Animal Protection Act. We ask whether horses should be entrusted to the army's care at all.
Producer: Michael Duffett
Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender
Research: Sinethemba Nogude

Script:


SANDF HORSES
 
Patrick Brown, a well-known horse trainer and equestrian champion had his passion for horses kindled when he joined the SADF equestrian unit in Potchestroom in 1987. The horses in this unit were highly prized.
 
Patrick: They had great facilities, great stables, the lacked for nothing, the best food, the best grass.
 
But in 2005 the SANDF equine unit was shut down.
 
Link: In 2011 the SADF decided to revive its equestrian unit, train horses and riders, to patrol our borders.
 
In 2018 veterinarian Dr Bryce Marock was at the base to check up on the horses .
 
Dr Marock: When we had arrived, we had realized that horses had already been shot, and we told that horses were being shot, due to collapse from emaciation.

 
So what went wrong in the intervening years? SINCE OCTOBER LAST YEAR, Lieutenant-Colonel Ernest Tlha/lerwa has headed up the South African Army Specialised Infantry Capability, or SAASIC for short, in Potchefstroom, which houses the equestrian unit. He says tenders were issued for specific types of horse required for border duty.

COL: The tenders, you are speaking to the suppliers you specify to them what type of horses you need what type of breed, age, trainer ability. There was no time to train you are only supposed to acquire and utilize.
 
The first group of 50 horses met the tender requirements.
 
DEV: So we were told initially that the first batch were trained horses but after that the other horses that arrived here were wild some were too old, too young, is that true?
 
COL: I think the first batch was fine, the second batch there was a little bit of a hick up because it was a different suppliers and it was a different personnel that source.
 
Tlha/lerwa says in total about 250 horses were bought, but it seems most were wild – and would have to be trained at the base.
 
Wendy Willson, is the NSPCA’s senior inspector, who has intimate knowledge of horses.
 
Wendy: I have been working with horses my whole life….My number one creature.
 
Wilson had been a member of the police equestrian unit, a stable manager and an instructor. In 2012 she read an article that raised concern about the welfare of the horses. She soon paid an unannounced visit to SAASIC but was denied entry.
 
Wendy: they did not want us on the base. They didn’t want us to inspect the horses [LEAVE OUT AS NOT OUT TO COLONEL and they didn’t want the public to know what is going on.  ]
 
Thla/lerwa sees it differently.
 
COL: The NSPCA were denied access because in the army we deal with polices and processes, you don’t sommer rock up.
Wilson obtained a High Court interdict to authorize her to enter the SAASIC compound.
 
The NSPCA then engaged with the SANDF to develop a joint memorandum of understanding on how the horses should be trained and cared for. The NSPCA provided training to SAAASIC members and were in constant touch with the base over the following years.
 
Some horses were moved around to other locations. But by 2017 the whole herd, which had grown in number, was reassembled in a SAASIC paddock. It was unsuited to cope with the numbers.
 
COL: When we had to feed there was a natural competition amongst the animals…so the bigger horses were bullying the smaller horses and there was no alternative like where we can say now, let me take the smaller horses and put them aside and feed them.
 
Losing patience, the NSPCA intensified its pressure. In December 2017 Dr Marock visited SAACIC.
 
MAROCK: The general state of the facilities that they were being kept in out the animals at high risk… that if one small cog in the wheel broke, something like this was going to happen.
 
Marock sent a letter to the SANDF warning them of a crisis, urging them to consider reducing the numbers in the herd.
 
LINK: Realizing that something had to be done, in April last year, the NSPCA arrived at SAASIC to negotiate the release of some of the horses into their care, according to them, what they found was distressing.
 
THEY SAW Horses starving, wandering around aimlessly and some had visible wounds.
 
MAROCK: When we arrived, in this area I had seen in December, the trees had all gone, they had eaten the branches even, there was so stool because as we had witnessed, the horses were eating horse stool.


 
COL : It never happened, I think they read it somewhere..
 
DEV: They saw it
 
COL In a natural way, horse will never eat its own feces, only a dog or a pig would
 
Tlha/lerwa denies that horses WERE STARVING AND THAT THEY ate the trees – the trees are still on the site, he says.
 
25 horses were in such bad shape that they had to be euthanized.
 
WENDY: I think the burden of responsibility should be every one on that base, everybody should have done something to ensure the welfare of those horses.
 
DEVI: So how did you feel when you saw those animals getting to a stage of they were did this not even we've gone past malnutrition. [00:22:15] So horses were starving. So how could you have fixed it
 
COL the way we could have fix it. It is to provide an alternative accommodation that was done later on
 
A few months later 60 horses were relocated to another army base.
 
DEVI: But why didn't you come up with that plan beforehand? Why did we had to find ourselves in a situation where [00:23:00] the horses were already starving. don't forget, horses were put down. so we mustn't make this sound as if it was just a small thing that happened. 
 
COL It was not the small thing because when you look at the pictures here it it was not a good thing, but that's what I'm saying. The plan was [00:23:15] put into place later on
 
DEVI: too late is what I'm saying...
 
Tlha/lerwa referred us to the SANDF national headquarters for the findings of a Board of Inquiry that was instituted last year into the state of the horses. The Board found the there was no starvation and enough food and water was available to the horses.
 
SAASIC agreed to release 69 horses into the custody of the NSPCA who had made sure that the horses were fed well enough to build their strength for the move. In July, the wild animals were finally loaded up, heading for a new home.
 
Link
While they were there the NSPCA happened to witness the training of some of the horses, the methods being used, in their minds, were unacceptable.
 
Wilson and her team saw 7 soldiers riding horses in a way the NSPCA deemed brutal.
 
WENDY: They were being kicked violently, to a degree that you can’t comprehend. The violence of the kick propelled the rider out of the saddle, one almost fell of.
 
COL: We have got our own curriculum as to how we train horses. According to them its terrible….
DEV: Don’t you think they should no, its their job
COL: The nspca know the welfare of the horse, not the training, especially when you say the military training of the horses.
 
The horses were shaved so that photographs could be taken of the extensive bruising caused by the kicking. Willson confiscated 7 horses AND SAID 2, over the age of 20, had to be put down. – ALLEGEDLY due to LONG TERM DAMAGE TO THEIR BVODIES. AND ADVANCED AGE.
 
The 69 horses were delivered to an equestrian center on a farm in Rietfontein, owned by Busisewe Sebi/lwane.
 
DEV: what were the conditions of the horses?
 
Busisewa: The conditions were very bad I must say… they were scared, they did not want to be touched, it was extremely bad, some of them were hurt.
 
The NSPCA was forced to euthanize 22 horses due to illness and permanent injuries they say were sustained at the base. A huge task lay ahead for Sebi/loane, her staff, volunteers and the NSPCA, to tame the remaining wild horses.
 
The horses that were transferred in June 2018 from Potchefstroom to the Rooiwal military base in Pretoria faced several challenges, including the high prevalence of African horse sickness in the area – which the NPCA’s Dr Marock had warned them about.  11 of the 60 horses died within 9 months.
 
COL: The 11 died…. Were for natural attrition, snake bites, and other conditions that could not be helped by the medics. Only one died of animal sickness.
 
The SANDF Board of inquiry recommended that Rooiwal needed to be developed as per Military Veterinaty Institute recommendations.
 
Meanwhile back at MISTY MEADOWS, amazing progress was being made with the horses that had begun to trust humans again.]
 
Busisiwe: The difference is magnificence, it is like a dream, it a totally different.
 
This is Sebil/woane’s daughter on BERRYBLITZ, once a wild horse - 
Within 8 MONTHS ALL the HORSES were ADOPTED by loving families, their futures now safe and secure.
 
Harry, once a wild mule, who was part of the SAASIC herd was adopted by Dawn Nicholson. Harry has free rein of her house. He has changed Dawn’s life.
 
The SANDF said in their statement that the procuremeent of a suitable farm and company of horses remained a er of priority, as recommended by the Board of Inquiry. At this stage 40 horses remain on the border, and 27 at the Saasic base.
 
Wilson has laid charges in terms of the Animal Protection Act at the Potchefstroom Police Station. After a year, Wilson is frustrated by a lack of progress.
 
COL: I am not aware of any police, since I come here since October, I have never come across police whi are wanting statements.
 
Wilson is determined to see this through. She hopes that a conviction will send a clear message.
 
WENDY: We can’t entrust to a place that shows so much disregard to a living breathing entity, we just cant.

Author Last Updated 19 May 2019 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 07 June 2019 Press Release: The SANDF’s Horses Starving, infected with various diseases and some eating their own faeces, over 25 horses have had to be put down after being in the care of the South African Army Special Infantry Capability Unit at the SANDF’s Potchefstroom base last year. A further 22 horses rescued from the base had to be euthanised as they were in such poor condition. Carte Blanche investigates why 11 of the 60 horses which the SANDF transferred to another army base in Pretoria have died and we visit some of the surviving horses that have been re-homed, while the NSPCA laid cruelty charges in terms of the Animal Protection Act. We ask whether horses should be entrusted to the army's care at all. Producer: Michael Duffett Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender Research: Sinethemba Nogude Script: SANDF HORSES Patrick Brown, a well-known horse trainer and equestrian champion had his passion for horses kindled when he joined the SADF equestrian unit in Potchestroom in 1987. The horses in this unit were highly prized. Patrick: They had great facilities, great stables, the lacked for nothing, the best food, the best grass. But in 2005 the SANDF equine unit was shut down. Link: In 2011 the SADF decided to revive its equestrian unit, train horses and riders, to patrol our borders. In 2018 veterinarian Dr Bryce Marock was at the base to check up on the horses . Dr Marock: When we had arrived, we had realized that horses had already been shot, and we told that horses were being shot, due to collapse from emaciation. So what went wrong in the intervening years? SINCE OCTOBER LAST YEAR, Lieutenant-Colonel Ernest Tlha/lerwa has headed up the South African Army Specialised Infantry Capability, or SAASIC for short, in Potchefstroom, which houses the equestrian unit. He says tenders were issued for specific types of horse required for border duty. COL: The tenders, you are speaking to the suppliers you specify to them what type of horses you need what type of breed, age, trainer ability. There was no time to train you are only supposed to acquire and utilize. The first group of 50 horses met the tender requirements. DEV: So we were told initially that the first batch were trained horses but after that the other horses that arrived here were wild some were too old, too young, is that true? COL: I think the first batch was fine, the second batch there was a little bit of a hick up because it was a different suppliers and it was a different personnel that source. Tlha/lerwa says in total about 250 horses were bought, but it seems most were wild – and would have to be trained at the base. Wendy Willson, is the NSPCA’s senior inspector, who has intimate knowledge of horses. Wendy: I have been working with horses my whole life….My number one creature. Wilson had been a member of the police equestrian unit, a stable manager and an instructor. In 2012 she read an article that raised concern about the welfare of the horses. She soon paid an unannounced visit to SAASIC but was denied entry. Wendy: they did not want us on the base. They didn’t want us to inspect the horses [LEAVE OUT AS NOT OUT TO COLONEL and they didn’t want the public to know what is going on. ] Thla/lerwa sees it differently. COL: The NSPCA were denied access because in the army we deal with polices and processes, you don’t sommer rock up. Wilson obtained a High Court interdict to authorize her to enter the SAASIC compound. The NSPCA then engaged with the SANDF to develop a joint memorandum of understanding on how the horses should be trained and cared for. The NSPCA provided training to SAAASIC members and were in constant touch with the base over the following years. Some horses were moved around to other locations. But by 2017 the whole herd, which had grown in number, was reassembled in a SAASIC paddock. It was unsuited to cope with the numbers. COL: When we had to feed there was a natural competition amongst the animals…so the bigger horses were bullying the smaller horses and there was no alternative like where we can say now, let me take the smaller horses and put them aside and feed them. Losing patience, the NSPCA intensified its pressure. In December 2017 Dr Marock visited SAACIC. MAROCK: The general state of the facilities that they were being kept in out the animals at high risk… that if one small cog in the wheel broke, something like this was going to happen. Marock sent a letter to the SANDF warning them of a crisis, urging them to consider reducing the numbers in the herd. LINK: Realizing that something had to be done, in April last year, the NSPCA arrived at SAASIC to negotiate the release of some of the horses into their care, according to them, what they found was distressing. THEY SAW Horses starving, wandering around aimlessly and some had visible wounds. MAROCK: When we arrived, in this area I had seen in December, the trees had all gone, they had eaten the branches even, there was so stool because as we had witnessed, the horses were eating horse stool. COL : It never happened, I think they read it somewhere.. DEV: They saw it COL In a natural way, horse will never eat its own feces, only a dog or a pig would Tlha/lerwa denies that horses WERE STARVING AND THAT THEY ate the trees – the trees are still on the site, he says. 25 horses were in such bad shape that they had to be euthanized. WENDY: I think the burden of responsibility should be every one on that base, everybody should have done something to ensure the welfare of those horses. DEVI: So how did you feel when you saw those animals getting to a stage of they were did this not even we've gone past malnutrition. [00:22:15] So horses were starving. So how could you have fixed it COL the way we could have fix it. It is to provide an alternative accommodation that was done later on A few months later 60 horses were relocated to another army base. DEVI: But why didn't you come up with that plan beforehand? Why did we had to find ourselves in a situation where [00:23:00] the horses were already starving. don't forget, horses were put down. so we mustn't make this sound as if it was just a small thing that happened. COL It was not the small thing because when you look at the pictures here it it was not a good thing, but that's what I'm saying. The plan was [00:23:15] put into place later on DEVI: too late is what I'm saying... Tlha/lerwa referred us to the SANDF national headquarters for the findings of a Board of Inquiry that was instituted last year into the state of the horses. The Board found the there was no starvation and enough food and water was available to the horses. SAASIC agreed to release 69 horses into the custody of the NSPCA who had made sure that the horses were fed well enough to build their strength for the move. In July, the wild animals were finally loaded up, heading for a new home. Link While they were there the NSPCA happened to witness the training of some of the horses, the methods being used, in their minds, were unacceptable. Wilson and her team saw 7 soldiers riding horses in a way the NSPCA deemed brutal. WENDY: They were being kicked violently, to a degree that you can’t comprehend. The violence of the kick propelled the rider out of the saddle, one almost fell of. COL: We have got our own curriculum as to how we train horses. According to them its terrible…. DEV: Don’t you think they should no, its their job COL: The nspca know the welfare of the horse, not the training, especially when you say the military training of the horses. The horses were shaved so that photographs could be taken of the extensive bruising caused by the kicking. Willson confiscated 7 horses AND SAID 2, over the age of 20, had to be put down. – ALLEGEDLY due to LONG TERM DAMAGE TO THEIR BVODIES. AND ADVANCED AGE. The 69 horses were delivered to an equestrian center on a farm in Rietfontein, owned by Busisewe Sebi/lwane. DEV: what were the conditions of the horses? Busisewa: The conditions were very bad I must say… they were scared, they did not want to be touched, it was extremely bad, some of them were hurt. The NSPCA was forced to euthanize 22 horses due to illness and permanent injuries they say were sustained at the base. A huge task lay ahead for Sebi/loane, her staff, volunteers and the NSPCA, to tame the remaining wild horses. The horses that were transferred in June 2018 from Potchefstroom to the Rooiwal military base in Pretoria faced several challenges, including the high prevalence of African horse sickness in the area – which the NPCA’s Dr Marock had warned them about. 11 of the 60 horses died within 9 months. COL: The 11 died…. Were for natural attrition, snake bites, and other conditions that could not be helped by the medics. Only one died of animal sickness. The SANDF Board of inquiry recommended that Rooiwal needed to be developed as per Military Veterinaty Institute recommendations. Meanwhile back at MISTY MEADOWS, amazing progress was being made with the horses that had begun to trust humans again.] Busisiwe: The difference is magnificence, it is like a dream, it a totally different. This is Sebil/woane’s daughter on BERRYBLITZ, once a wild horse - Within 8 MONTHS ALL the HORSES were ADOPTED by loving families, their futures now safe and secure. Harry, once a wild mule, who was part of the SAASIC herd was adopted by Dawn Nicholson. Harry has free rein of her house. He has changed Dawn’s life. The SANDF said in their statement that the procuremeent of a suitable farm and company of horses remained a er of priority, as recommended by the Board of Inquiry. At this stage 40 horses remain on the border, and 27 at the Saasic base. Wilson has laid charges in terms of the Animal Protection Act at the Potchefstroom Police Station. After a year, Wilson is frustrated by a lack of progress. COL: I am not aware of any police, since I come here since October, I have never come across police whi are wanting statements. Wilson is determined to see this through. She hopes that a conviction will send a clear message. WENDY: We can’t entrust to a place that shows so much disregard to a living breathing entity, we just cant. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): should horses be entrusted into the care of the SANDF?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In Aug 2018 the Nspca were horrified to discover that horses in the care of the SANDF at their equine base called SAASIC in Potchestroom army base were starving to death. Over 200 hundred horses had been purchased by the army for the new SAASIC unit - these horses were to be trained for border patrol. There is a long history with regard to horses in the SANDF, going back to their use in border patrol in the 1970's and 1980"s. The unit had been disbanded and the police took over the care of horses for their use. Then SAASIC was formed in 2014. Most of the horses that were bought were not tame. and the NSPCA offered help to the army. to help train the horses. This was turned down. They heard reports of the animals being mistreated and went to investigate. many of the horses were not being fed...and some were in such bad condition that 25 had to be put down immediately., Whilst the NCPCA were there they saw army riding horses in a cruel way, and they filmed this. 2 charges were laid for animal cruelty. They also got a court order preventing the riders from riding these horses. The NSPCA did a deal with the Army and took over the care of 76 horses which they re-homed. In a matter of months these untame horses became tame. A vet did an experiment on the horses back at the base. The vet showed different uniforms to the horses that had been abused..the only uniform that the horses reacted badly to was sandf uniforms. The SANDF insisted on keeping some horses at their base but against the advice of the NSPCA, the SANDF sent 60 to an army base called Rooiwal, better conditions. They were warned about this because of the high incidence of equine sickness in the area. The army insisted. 20 horses died with the year from equine sickness and many broke their legs because if then rough terrain. Its been a year since charges were laid but the progress of the investigation has been hampered by lack of SANDF o-operation. A commission of enquiry was held apparently by the army into the starving horses but the results of this enquiry were not released. There is a rumour that the SANDF paid top dollar for trained horses but instead they received untrained horses.,
metadata.Summary: There is a natural narrative - and the overriding theme is the care and protection of animals whether they are in service or our pets. We expect the state to set an example. The SANDF's treatment of these horses is nothing short of a scandalous. Two charges against the SANDF speaks volumes. Our story line should send shivers down the spine of our viewers and it is hoped that there will be such an outcry that radical attitude changes will result at the SANDF.
